qs-governance.rationale: All institution types need AI governance. Research-intensive institutions have more complex governance needs. Teaching-focused institutions may prioritise simpler, faster governance.

qs-outreach.rationale: Teaching-focused institutions and polytechnics depend more heavily on recruitment and student support. Research-intensive institutions may invest less in outreach AI.

qs-teaching.rationale: Teaching-focused institutions have the strongest mission alignment with this pillar. Research-intensive institutions may deprioritise teaching AI investment.

qs-research.rationale: Research-intensive institutions have fundamentally different expectations for AI research capability. Teaching-focused institutions may legitimately score lower here.

calibration_notes: When interpreting scores, acknowledge that institution type creates different baseline expectations. A teaching-focused institution scoring Basic on Research is less concerning than a research-intensive institution scoring Basic. Never suggest all institution types should aim for the same profile.

qs-governance.rationale: AI regulation varies dramatically by region. EU AI Act creates mandatory compliance; UK takes a pro-innovation approach; US has sectoral regulation. Governance requirements differ fundamentally.

qs-outreach.rationale: Recruitment markets and data protection regimes vary by region but the core AI outreach capabilities are similar.

qs-teaching.rationale: Quality assurance frameworks vary by region but AI teaching capabilities are broadly transferable.

qs-research.rationale: Research funding landscapes differ but AI research capability requirements are similar. Infrastructure availability may vary.

calibration_notes: Regional context is critical for the Governance pillar. An EU institution must meet EU AI Act requirements that a US institution does not face. Never compare governance scores across regions without acknowledging regulatory context. Region also affects infrastructure availability: institutions in lower-income regions may face infrastructure constraints that limit Advanced scores even with excellent strategy.

qs-governance.rationale: Institutions with operational AI but no governance are a common high-risk pattern. Governance maturity should match or exceed AI usage maturity.

qs-outreach.rationale: AI maturity baseline predicts readiness for outreach AI adoption but does not determine capability.

qs-teaching.rationale: Baseline affects how quickly teaching AI can be deployed but pedagogic readiness is an independent factor.

qs-research.rationale: Research AI capability builds on existing infrastructure and skills. No-AI-use institutions face a larger capability gap.

calibration_notes: The most important diagnostic pattern is governance-usage mismatch: institutions with operational AI use but Basic governance are at risk. Flag this pattern whenever detected.

qs-governance.rationale: Large institutions face coordination challenges. Small institutions may lack specialist capacity. Medium institutions often balance these well.

qs-outreach.rationale: Large institutions have volumes that justify AI investment. Small institutions may benefit from AI to compensate for limited staff.

qs-teaching.rationale: Teaching AI capability is relatively size-independent. Pedagogic innovation can happen at any scale.

qs-research.rationale: Large institutions can invest in comprehensive AI research infrastructure. Small institutions must be selective.

calibration_notes: Size affects the speed and cost of implementation, not the target level. Never suggest that small institutions cannot achieve Advanced capability; they achieve it differently.

qs-governance.rationale: AI governance needs are similar regardless of sector focus. Humanities institutions may bring stronger ethical governance perspectives.

qs-outreach.rationale: Outreach AI capabilities are largely sector-independent.

qs-teaching.rationale: AI in teaching looks fundamentally different across sectors. STEM may adopt tools faster; humanities face distinctive challenges around writing, critical analysis, and creativity.

qs-research.rationale: STEM institutions have natural advantages in AI research. Humanities institutions contribute differently (AI ethics, AI impact, critical AI studies). Both are valid but look different.

calibration_notes: STEM-heavy institutions will naturally score higher on Research AI and may adopt Teaching AI tools faster. Humanities-heavy institutions may score higher on AI ethics, critical perspectives, and AI scholarship. Neither pattern is inherently better. Avoid framing STEM patterns as the norm.

qs-governance.rationale: Only senior leadership and CIO have full visibility of institutional AI governance. Academic leaders see their faculty. Professional services leaders see operational governance.

qs-outreach.rationale: Professional services leaders have the best visibility of outreach AI. Academic leaders may have limited visibility of recruitment and support operations.

qs-teaching.rationale: Academic leaders have direct visibility of teaching practice. CIOs see infrastructure but not pedagogic reality. Senior leaders may see strategy but not classroom practice.

qs-research.rationale: Research leaders have the best visibility of research AI practice. CIOs see infrastructure. Other roles have limited visibility of research practice.

calibration_notes: Always note the respondent's role and flag where their visibility may be limited. A CIO assessing teaching practice, or an academic leader assessing governance, should be treated with lower confidence for those pillars. Ideal assessment combines multiple respondent perspectives.

qs-governance.rationale: Governance capability can be assessed regardless of personal AI familiarity. The question is whether institutional structures exist.

qs-outreach.rationale: Outreach AI capability is about institutional practice, not individual familiarity.

qs-teaching.rationale: Low-familiarity respondents may not recognise AI tools in use or understand what AI-enhanced teaching looks like. They may underestimate institutional capability.

qs-research.rationale: Low-familiarity respondents may not recognise AI in research practice. High-familiarity respondents may overestimate institutional capability based on their own advanced use.

calibration_notes: Low-familiarity respondents may underestimate capability (they do not recognise AI in use). High-familiarity respondents may overestimate institutional capability (they project their own practice). Moderate familiarity is the most reliable. Flag extreme familiarity levels as potential bias sources.
